newsitem.title: USA: Fischler urges more market-oriented EU farm policy.
newsitem.headline: Fischler urges more market-oriented EU farm policy.

text.p: European Union agriculutural policy must become more market-oriented or it risks generating huge unexportable surpluses of beef, grain and dairy products by the middle of next decade, a top E.U. official said Monday.

In a speech sponsored by the European Institute, E.U. Agriculture Commissioner Franz Fischler said the E.U. must further reduce its reliance on commodity price supports as a means of boosting farm income.
It also must "wean (agricultural) exports away from the dependence on export subsidies," he said.

Fischler was in Washington for talks with U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky, US Agriculture Department Secretary Dan Glickman and the chairmen of the House and Senate Agriculture Committees.
The EU Commission will release a set of recommendations for agricultural policy reform in mid-July.

In his speech, Fischler said the E.U. must go even further in its next round of Common Agricultural Policy reform than it did in 1992, when market price supports were reduced and replaced with direct payments to farmers and an acreage setaside program was implemented to help manage supplies.
"It is already clear that the considerable acheivements of our 1992 reform will fade in the light of new problems as time goes by," Fischler said.

Without further reform, the E.U. is likely to generate surpluses of grain, beef, wine and olive oil that it will have difficulty exporting because of limits on export subsidies under the Uruguay Round international trade pact, he said.

Fischler called for an even "greater separation of market and income policies" than began in 1992. In that regard, future E.U. support to be farmers should be more in the form of direct payments--such as for adopting certain environmental practices--than "artificially high" price supports, he said.
Enlargement of the European Union to include up to 10 new members from Central and Eastern Europe also adds to the pressure for additional CAP reform, Fischler said.

But rather than extending direct payments to an estimated 10 million farmers in the 10 applicant countries, assistance will likely take the form of increased investment in the food industry and strengthening food safety standards, he said.
"I think such a concept would be acceptable" to Eastern and Central European farmers since they will enjoy higher prices for their products as a result of joining the E.U., he said.
The E.U. expects to add its first new members from Central and Eastern Europe by early next decade, Fischler said.
